column2: In the morning, having bathed duly, one should worship the lord of the gods with perfumes and other offerings and heaps of food offerings,
then duly feed the invited brahmins, O brahmin, and likewise feed others who come, and the poor and helpless.
This Shakra vow, O brahmin, should be performed every year by a king or another wealthy man who desires a good harvest.
On the full moon of the month of Ashvina is the vow called Kojagara: bathing duly, fasting and with senses controlled,
one should worship a golden Lakshmi placed on a copper or earthen pitcher, clothed, with various offerings.
Then in the evening, when the lord of stars has risen, one should light lamps of gold, silver or clay filled with ghee —
a lakh, half that, ten thousand, a thousand or a hundred — and cooking plenty of milk-rice mixed with ghee and sugar,
placing it in many vessels in the moonlight of the cool-rayed moon, when a watch of the night has passed, one should offer it to Lakshmi.
Then one should feed brahmins with it devotedly and keep vigil with them, with dance, song and auspicious things.
Then at dawn, having bathed, one should give that image to the teacher. On this night Mahalakshmi, her lotus hands in the gestures of boon and fearlessness,
wanders the world at midnight: "Who is awake on earth? To my worshipper who is awake I give wealth."
This vow that pleases Lakshmi, kept year after year, grants prosperity in this world and, at the body's end, in the next.
On the full moon of Kartika one should behold Kartika, to gain brahminhood again and to conquer all enemies.
On this same day the festival of Tripura should be held with the gift of lamps at nightfall, O best of brahmins, bringing happiness to all living beings.
Insects, moths, mosquitoes and trees, and the beings that move in water and on land — seeing the lamps, they are not born again, but surely attain liberation.
Here, at moonrise, O brahmin, the six Krittikas should be worshipped,
and Karttikeya, the sword-bearer, Varuna and Fire, with perfumes, flowers, incense, lamps and abundant food offerings,
with fine food, fruits, vegetables, and satisfying fire and brahmins; having worshipped the gods thus, one should place a lamp outside the house.
Near the lamp a pleasing square pit fourteen fingers wide should be made and sprinkled with sandal water;
filling it with cow's milk, one should place in it a golden fish with pearl eyes, beautiful in every part,
uttering the mantra "Salutations to the great Fish," and worshipping it there with perfumes and the like, one should give it to a brahmin.
The gift of the ocean of milk has been told you, O best of brahmins; by the power of this gift one rejoices in Hari's presence.
Here, releasing a bull and keeping the night vow, O Narada, one attains Rudra's world; there is no doubt.
On the full moon of Margashirsha one should give an adhaka of salt with gold to a peaceful brahmin for the fulfilment of all desires.
Long ago this world was abandoned by Lakshmi; then Hari, Purandara, Soma, Tishya and Brihaspati —
these five, on the full moon joined with Pushya, by force adorned the world again with festivities of good fortune.
So a man, at the conjunction with Pushya, for the increase of all good fortune, anointing his body with a paste of white mustard,
should bathe with water of all herbs and wear new garments; seeing, touching and bowing to auspicious things, he should then worship
Hari, Shakra, Indu, Pushya and Brihaspati with perfumes and other offerings, perform an oblation, and satisfy brahmins with milk-rice.
Having kept this vow, O brahmin, which increases Rama's pleasure and destroys misfortune, one rejoices here and hereafter.
Then on the full moon of Magha, giving sesame, cotton, blankets, gems, jackets, turbans, sandals or wealth
according to one's means, one rejoices in heaven. Whoever worships the god Shankara duly here
gains the fruit of the horse-sacrifice and is honoured in Vishnu's world. On the full moon of Phalguna the worship of Holika is prescribed:
one should have a heap of all kinds of wood and cow-dung cakes made; kindling fire there duly with many rakshasa-slaying mantras,
O Holi, you were made by foolish ones terrified of the blood-drinkers; so I will worship you; O Being, be the giver of prosperity —
lighting it with this mantra and casting in wood and the like, circumambulating, one should hold a festival with the sound of songs and instruments.
This Holika was a rakshasi who frightened Prahlada; so they burn her thus with wood and the like and auspicious songs.
It is the burning of the year; in another view, the burning of Kama. Know, O best of brahmins, that custom in the world is manifold.
At the end of the fortnight there are two separate ones; then the vow of the new moon is told; hear it separately from me, O brahmin, very dear to the ancestors.
In Chaitra and Vaishakha, on the new moon, one should worship the ancestors with shraddha by the parvana procedure according to one's means,
feeding brahmins and giving gifts, especially of cows and the like, since the new moon in every month gives great merit.
On the new moon of Jyeshtha the vow of Savitri is declared, O Narada; its procedure is declared here too, like that of the full moon of Jyeshtha.
In the months of Shuchi, Nabhas and Bhadra, at the end of the month, O brahmin, shraddha to the ancestors, gifts, oblations and worship of the gods become endless.
On the new moon of Bhadra, in the afternoon, kusha grass grown in a sesame field, cut with the mantra of Viranchi and 'hum phat,' O brahmin,
one should use in all rites always, and others only once. On the new moon of Isha especially, shraddha and libations to the ancestors
should be performed in the water of the Jahnavi, and at Gaya it grants liberation. On the new moon of Urja, the gift of lamps in temples,
at rivers, gardens and tanks, at shrines, cowsheds and markets, and the worship of Lakshmi in wrought and unwrought gold and silver;
and gambling foretells the year's fruit, in victory or defeat. The worship of cows is prescribed here, colouring their horns and other limbs,
with gifts of fodder, food and the like, salutations and circumambulation. In Margashirsha too there should be worship of the ancestors with shraddhas and feeding of brahmins,
with disciplines such as celibacy, and japa, oblation, worship and the like. In Pausha and Magha, O best of brahmins, shraddha to the ancestors gives greater fruit;
on the new moon joined with Karna, Pata and the sun it surpasses Gaya. In Phalguna, only shraddha and feeding of brahmins,
and gifts and the like give all fruits; on the new moon on a Monday the fruit is greater. Thus in brief the duties of the lunar days have been told you, O sage;
everywhere there are special points, found in other Puranas.

he saw a banyan like a dark cloud, a hundred yojanas wide; beneath it, seated in the midst of a circle of yogis,
the one with matted locks, the misshapen-eyed, clad in a tiger skin, his whole body adorned with ash, adorned with serpent ornaments,
ever beautiful with a rosary of rudraksha, crowned with the moon — seeing him, Narada, O brahmins, his neck bowed in devotion,
bowed his head at the feet of the Lord of the world; then, praising the bull-bannered one with glad heart and words,
he sat down at Sthanu's command, honoured then by the yogis. Then the teacher of the worlds asked Narada about his welfare,
and he said, "By your grace I have everything." As all the best yogis listened there, O brahmins,
he asked about Shambhu's knowledge, which releases the soul from its bonds; and Shiva, his heart pleased by his devotion, respectfully
taught him the yoga with eight limbs, being kind to those who bow. Having received Shambhu's knowledge from Shankara, who brings good to the world,
he bowed with a most glad heart and went to Narayana; there too Narada, constantly going and coming,
pleased Narayana, served by yogis and Siddhas. This great Naradiya I have told you, O brahmins,
a narrative equal to the Veda, displaying all scriptures, in four parts, increasing the knowledge of those who hear it.
Whoever recites this Naradiya, O brahmins, in a Shiva temple, in an assembly of eminent brahmins, or in a temple of Keshava,
at Mathura, at Prayaga, in the presence of Purushottama, at the Setu, at Kanchi, at Kushasthali, at Gangadvara, at Kushasthala,
at the Pushkaras, on a river bank, or wherever, with devotion, gains the great fruit of all sacrifices and tirthas,
of all gifts and all austerities without remainder. Fasting, or eating only sacrificial food, with senses controlled,
the hearer and likewise the speaker, devoted to Narayana or delighting in devotion to Shiva, gains success by hearing it.
In it is declared the source of all merits and siddhis; it always destroys all sins for those who read and hear it,
removes men's faults of the Kali age, increases all prosperity, is desired by all and illuminates all knowledge
for Shaivas, Vaishnavas, Shaktas, worshippers of the Sun and likewise Ganapatyas, and those in the classes and stages of life, O brahmins;
it illuminates the fruits of austerities and vows, and, division by division, of mantras, yantras and the limbs of the Veda,
and it is a compendium of the Agamas, the Sankhyas and the Vedas. Whoever reads this with devotion or hears it with concentration
gains the desires he wishes, rare even among the gods. Having heard this Naradiya Purana, equal to the Veda,
one should devotedly honour the reciter with wealth, gems, clothes and the like; with gifts of land, cows and gems constantly,
and gifts of elephants, horses and chariots, one should always please the teacher. The one who expounds, O brahmins, the Purana, the compendium of dharma,
which grants men the four aims — what other teacher is his equal? In body, mind and speech, and with wealth and the like, constantly
one should do what is dear to that teacher who teaches dharma. Having heard the Purana duly, performed an oblation and worshipped the gods,
one should then feed a hundred brahmins with sweet food and milk-rice and give fees according to one's means; with devotion Madhava is pleased.
As the Ganga is the best of rivers, Pushkara of lakes, Kashi of cities, Meru of mountains, Narayana Hari of gods,
the Krita of ages, the Sama of Vedas, the cow, the brahmin, food and water, the month of Margashirsha, the lion, the man, the ashvattha, Prahlada, the face,
Ucchaihshravas, spring, japa, Shesha, Aryaman, the bow, Fire, Vishnu, Indra, Kapila, the lord of speech, the poet,
Arjuna, Hanuman, darbha, the mind, Chitraratha, the lotus, Urvashi and gold — as these are the best of their kinds,
so the Naradiya is proclaimed among the Puranas. Peace and good be with all of you, O best of brahmins;
I shall go to my teacher Vyasa of boundless radiance." Having said this, Suta, honoured by the great-souled Shaunaka and the others,
and given leave again by all, went to see his teacher; and all those best of brahmins led by Shaunaka, collected, practising well what they had heard, remained there at the sacrificial session.
Whoever, using the medicine of japa and worship, serves Hari, who destroys the poison of the sins of Kali, comes to the sacrifice with a mind free of poison and gains the world he desires.
Let us quickly leave this place and go elsewhere without delay, so that there is no more talk with this ignorant one.
Salutations to Shri Ganesha.
Salutations to Shri Gauri and Shankara.

The glorious Shiva Mahapurana, third book, the Shatarudra Samhita, chapter 34: the description of Shiva's incarnation called Sunartaka-Nata. Nandishvara said: "O all-knowing Sanatkumara, hear of the incarnation of the all-pervading Shiva, the Supreme Self, called Sunartaka-Nata (the fine dancer).
[Parvati said:] "Fulfil my desire, O Lord; you are always changeless. You bear the name 'kind to devotees,' and I am always your devotee."
Nandishvara said: Addressed thus by her, Shambhu, Mahesha, kind to devotees, said, "So be it," vanished, and went to his own mountain.
Parvati too, joyfully, with her two friends, went to her father's house, her form made fruitful.
Hearing of Parvati's arrival, Himachala with Mena and his family went joyfully to see his daughter.
Seeing her with a radiant face, they brought her home, and with great delight and love they held a great festival.
Mena and the lord of mountains gave wealth to brahmins and others, and had auspicious rites performed with the sound of the Vedas, reverently.
Then Mena stayed joyfully in the courtyard with her daughter, and the mountain Himavat went to bathe in the Ganga.
Meanwhile Shambhu, of beautiful sport and kind to his devotees, became a fine dancer and went to Menaka.
Holding a horn in his left hand and a damaru in his right, with a patched cloak on his back and red garments, skilled in dance and song,
in the form of a dancer he joyfully performed in Menaka's courtyard various dances and most charming songs.
When the Goddess Kalika, Parvati, daughter of Himavat, went to the forest and performed very pure austerity to win Shiva,
He played the horn and damaru there with fine sound and joyfully made various charming displays.
All the townspeople, men and women, children and even the old, came there at once to see him.
Hearing the fine song and seeing the charming dance, all were suddenly enchanted, and Mena too, O sage.
Then Mena quickly went, with heart delighted by his show, to give him jewels in golden vessels.
He did not accept them: "I seek alms — Shiva (Parvati) herself," and he made ready again, playfully, to dance and sing.
Hearing his words, Mena, greatly astonished, grew very angry; she rebuked the mendicant and wanted to drive him out.
Meanwhile the king of mountains came from the Ganga and saw before him the mendicant in human form standing in the courtyard.
Hearing the whole matter from Mena's mouth, he grew very angry and ordered his attendants to put the mendicant out.
But no one could put him out, O best of sages, for he blazed like a great fire, hard to touch, full of radiance.
Then that mendicant, skilled in many sports, dear one, showed the mountain his infinite power.
The mountain saw him there at once bearing the form of Vishnu, then the form of Brahma, then in a moment the form of the Sun;
then he saw him, dear one, in the most wondrous form of Rudra, lovely, with Parvati, laughing and full of radiance.
Thus he saw there his very many forms, and was at once astonished and flooded with supreme bliss.
Then that best of mendicants, the creator, asked him and her for alms — Durga herself — and accepted nothing else.
Then the Supreme Lord in the form of the mendicant vanished and quickly went to his own abode, impelled by Durga's words.
Then true understanding came to Mena and the lord of mountains: "The Lord Shiva has deceived us and gone to his abode.
Our daughter Parvati, rich in austerity, should be given to him." Reflecting thus, supreme devotion to Shiva arose in them.
Therefore Rudra, having made a great display that delighted his devotees, joyfully married Parvati according to rule.
Thus, dear one, I have told you of Shiva's incarnation called Sunartaka-Nata, which fulfilled Shiva's (Parvati's) words.
This sinless, supreme narrative has been told by me; whoever hears it with love becomes happy and attains the goal.
Then Shiva was pleased with her fine austerity, O sage, and to test her conduct well he joyfully went to grant her a boon.
Well pleased at heart, he showed her his true form, and Shankara said to that Shiva, "Choose a boon," O sage.
Hearing Shambhu's words and seeing his excellent form, Shiva (Parvati) rejoiced greatly and, bowing low, said to him:
Parvati said: "If you are pleased, Lord of gods, and a boon is to be given me, be my husband, Ishana; show me grace.
With your leave I shall go properly to my father's house; you must come to my father, O Lord and master,
and ask for me as a mendicant, making your auspicious fame known; lovingly make my father's household life wholly fruitful.
Then, O Lord, you should hold the marriage by the procedure described, Maheshana, for the accomplishment of the gods' purpose."
Salutations to Shri Ganesha.
Salutations to Shri Gauri and Shankara.

The glorious Shiva Mahapurana, third book, the Shatarudra Samhita, chapter 35: the description of Shiva's incarnation as the pious brahmin. Nandishvara said: "O all-knowing Sanatkumara, hear of the incarnation of the all-pervading Shiva, the Supreme Self, called the brahmin in the guise of a holy man.
Hearing the gods' words, [Brihaspati] reflected and said to them:
The teacher said: "Let one of you go to the mountain, O gods, and accomplish what you desire; I am unable to do it.
Or else go, O gods, with Vasava, to Brahma's world; tell him your situation and he will do your work."
Nandishvara said: Hearing this and consulting together, the gods went to Brahma's assembly and told the whole matter before the Creator.
Hearing their words and reflecting well, Brahma said to them: "I will not revile him; that always brings sorrow and destroys happiness.
O gods, go to Kailasa and please Shankara; send that god to Himalaya's house.
Let him go to the lord of mountains and speak ill of himself; reviling others leads to ruin, but reviling oneself is held to bring fame."
Nandishvara said: Then all the gods quickly went to Kailasa, bowed to Shiva with devotion and told him the whole matter.
Hearing the gods' words, Maheshvara agreed; laughing, he reassured the gods and sent them away.
Then the blessed Shambhu, Mahesha, kind to devotees, lord of maya and without change, wished to go to the foot of the mountain.
Knowing the supreme devotion of Mena and Himalaya to Shiva, all the gods grew anxious and took counsel respectfully:
With staff and umbrella, in divine garments, wearing a bright tilaka, a crystal rosary in his hand and a shalagrama at his neck,
chanting Hari's name with devotion, a brahmin in the guise of a holy man, he quickly went to Himachala, who was with his kinsmen.
Seeing him, Himalaya rose with his attendants and prostrated himself on the ground like a staff, fully and duly.
Then the lord of mountains asked that brahmin, "Who are you?" and the best of brahmins answered the mountain at once with great respect:
The holy brahmin said: "I am called the holy brahmin, O mountain, a Vaishnava who sees the highest truth, a benefactor of others, all-knowing, going everywhere by my teacher's power.
I have learned by my own knowledge, while in my own place, O best of mountains — hear it; I tell it to you with love, putting aside pretence:
you wish to give your own daughter, lovely as Padma, to Shankara, whose family and conduct are unknown.
This intention of yours, lord of mountains, is not fitting or auspicious; understand, best of the wise, born of Narayana's line.
Consider your lordship over mountains — he has not a single kinsman. Ask your kinsmen carefully, and Mena, your beloved;
ask all of them carefully, Mena and the rest, but not Parvati; to a sick man, O mountain, medicine is never pleasing, but bad food always is.
He is not a fit match for you in the gift of Parvati; the great will smile merely on hearing of it.
He is without shelter, ever unattached, ugly, without qualities, changeless, a dweller in cremation grounds, fearsome, a snake-handler, naked,
adorned with ash, his head wound with great serpents, fallen from all stages of life, his course always unknown."
Brahma said: Having spoken these and other true words devoted to reviling Shiva, Shiva, the performer of many sports, quickly went to his own abode.
Hearing the brahmin's words, the two were stricken: "What shall we do, now that it has turned so contrary and harmful?"
Then Rudra, having made a great display that delighted his devotees, married Girija and accomplished the gods' purpose.
Thus, dear one, I have told you of Shiva's incarnation called the brahmin in holy guise, who accomplished the gods' purpose, O Lord.
This sinless narrative leads to heaven and gives long life; whoever reads or hears it becomes happy and attains the goal.

If the mountain, with single-minded devotion, gives his daughter to Shambhu, he will surely attain liberation at once from Shiva.
shivpurana:7:35.4	If he, the support of endless jewels, goes to liberation, the earth's name 'Ratnagarbha' (womb of jewels) will surely become false.
shivpurana:7:35.5	Giving up his immobility and taking a divine form, having given his daughter to the trident-bearer, he will go to Shiva's world;
shivpurana:7:35.6	gaining likeness to Mahadeva by Shambhu's grace, and enjoying great pleasures there, he will then attain liberation.
Having reflected thus, all the gods went to their teacher's house, O sage, and, seeking their own ends, made their request to the teacher.
The gods said: "Teacher, go to Himalaya's house to accomplish our purpose; reviling Mahesha, turn the mountain from his devotion.
If that mountain gives his daughter to Shiva out of faith, he would gain liberation right here, O teacher; let him rather remain on earth."
Salutations to Shri Ganesha.
Salutations to Shri Gauri and Shankara.

The glorious Shiva Mahapurana, third book, the Shatarudra Samhita, chapter 36: the description of Shiva's incarnation as Ashvatthama. Nandishvara said: "O all-knowing Sanatkumara, hear of the supreme incarnation of the all-pervading Shiva, the Supreme Self, called Ashvatthama.
Hearing Shambhu's words, Drona, bowing, said, "Give me a son born of your own portion, invincible to all and of great strength."
Hearing Drona's words, Shambhu said, "So be it," and vanished, dear one — the playful one who brings happiness, O sage.
Drona went to his own abode greatly delighted, his confusion gone, and joyfully told his wife all that had happened.
Then, when the time came, Rudra, the lord who ends all, was born by his own portion as Drona's son of great strength.
He became famous on earth as Ashvatthama, O sage, a great hero with lotus-petal eyes, destroyer of the enemy's side.
Famous in the Bharata war, he received his father's command and became a helper of the Kauravas, mighty one.
Relying on that great hero, the mighty Kauravas led by Bhishma became invincible even to the gods.
For fear of him all the Pandavas, great heroes and skilled though they were, were unable to conquer the Kauravas and were lost.
On Krishna's advice Arjuna performed most severe austerity to Shambhu, obtained a weapon by Shambhu's boon, and then conquered them.
Ashvatthama, the great hero born of Mahadeva's portion, O sage, nevertheless, subject to devotion to him, showed his own prowess.
From a portion of Brihaspati, the greatly wise divine sage, O sage, Drona was born of Bharadvaja, not from a womb, self-possessed —
having slain the sons of the Pandavas, though carefully trained, his strength irresistible even to Krishna and other great heroes,
seeing Arjuna, distraught with grief for his sons, rushing at him in his chariot with Achyuta, he fled,
and he released upon him the weapon called Brahmashiras; from it arose a fierce radiance in every direction.
Seeing danger to life, Arjuna, in distress, exhausted, his radiance gone and in great fear, said to Krishna:
Arjuna said: "What is this, and from where? Krishna, Krishna, I do not know; this unbearable radiance comes from every side."
Nandishvara said: Hearing Arjuna's words, Krishna, best of Shaivas, meditated on Shiva with his consort and replied to Arjuna respectfully:
Shri Krishna said: "Know this is the most terrible Brahma weapon of Drona's son; no other weapon can counter it.
Quickly remember Shiva, Shambhu, your lord, protector of devotees, who gave you his own supreme weapon that accomplishes every task.
Destroy the surging radiance of that weapon with the radiance of that Shaiva weapon." Having said this, Krishna himself meditated on Shiva for that purpose.
Hearing Krishna's words, Partha remembered Shiva in his heart, touched water, bowed and quickly released the weapon, O sage.
best of bowmen, heroic, a brahmin sage knowing all scriptures, of great fame and radiance, the best knower of all weapons,
Though the Brahmashiras weapon is unfailing and without counter, it was at once quelled by the radiance of the Shaiva weapon, O great sage.
Do not think this a wonder in Shiva, who is made of all wonders, the unborn one who by his own power creates, protects and destroys the whole universe.
Then Ashvatthama, born of Shiva's portion, knowing this Shaiva event, was not at all troubled, his mind content with Shiva's will, O sage.
Then Drona's son resolved to make this whole world free of Pandavas and to destroy the child in Uttara's womb.
That mighty lord hurled at Uttara's womb the Brahma weapon, of great radiance, irresistible by other weapons.
Then Uttara, wife of Jishnu's son, distraught in mind and burning from that weapon, praised Krishna, lord of Lakshmi.
Then Krishna, meditating on Shiva, praising him in his heart and bowing, understood that Drona's son's weapon was meant to make the world free of Pandavas.
With the brilliant Sudarshana weapon given by Indra for his own protection, he protected her by Shiva's command.
[Ashvatthama,] knowing what Krishna, the best of Shaivas, had done at Shankara's command, slowly became downcast.
Then Krishna, glad at heart, made all the Pandavas fall at his feet to please him, the king of Shaivas.
whom the wise know as expert in the science of the bow and in the Veda, the best, of wondrous deeds, Drona, who increased his family.
Then Drona's son, his heart pleased, lovingly gave various boons to the Pandavas and Krishna, and showed them grace.
Thus, dear one, the Lord Maheshvara performed supreme sport, descending to earth in the form of Drona's son, O best of sages.
Ashvatthama, Shiva's incarnation, of great strength and valour, who gives happiness to the three worlds, still lives on the bank of the Jahnavi.
The Ashvatthama incarnation of Lord Shankara has been described to you; it brings all success and grants the fruit devotees desire.
Whoever hears this with devotion or recites it with concentration gains the success he wishes and at the end goes to Shiva's city.
By his own strength he was the teacher of the Kauravas, O brahmin, famous among the six great chariot-warriors among the Kauravas.
To help the Kauravas, Dronacharya, best of brahmins, performed great austerity directed to Shiva for the sake of a son.
Then the blessed Shankara, kind to devotees, was pleased and appeared before Drona, O best of sages.
Seeing him, the brahmin Drona bowed quickly and praised him, his heart greatly gladdened, bowed low with folded hands.
Pleased by his praise and austerity, the Lord Shankara, kind to devotees, said to Drona, "Choose a boon."
Salutations to Shri Ganesha.
Salutations to Shri Gauri and Shankara.

The glorious Shiva Mahapurana, third book, the Shatarudra Samhita, chapter 37: the description of Vyasa's instruction. Nandishvara said: "Hear, wise one, of the incarnation of the Pinaka-bearer called Kirata, who killed Muka and, pleased, gave a boon to Arjuna.
Then the Pandavas asked Krishna, "What will happen? A mighty enemy has arisen; tell us what to do, O Lord."
Nandishvara said: Asked thus by the Pandavas, O sage, Shri Krishna remembered Shiva's lotus feet and said this to the Pandavas:
Shri Krishna said: "Listen, best of Pandavas, and having heard, act; hear especially my own story, joined with the service of Shiva.
Going to Dvaraka, wishing to conquer my enemies, and considering the instructions of the great-souled Upamanyu,
I worshipped Shambhu, and the Supreme Lord was pleased; I served him well for seven months on the excellent mountain Batuka,
and the Lord of the universe himself, present there, granted me the desires I wished; by his power I gained the highest capability.
Even now I serve the god who grants the fruit of enjoyment and liberation; you too serve that Shambhu, who brings all happiness."
Nandishvara said: Having said this and reassured the Pandavas, Krishna vanished and quickly went to Dvaraka, remembering Shiva's lotus feet.
The Pandavas then sent a Bhilla vigorously to test the qualities of Duryodhana.
He, learning all about Duryodhana's rising virtues there and finding them sound, came back to his masters.
Those excellent Pandavas, conquered by Suyodhana, came with the virtuous Draupadi to the forest called Dvaita.
Hearing what he told, they fell into sorrow, O lord of sages, and the Pandavas, greatly grieved, said to one another:
What should we do now, and where should we go for battle? Though all of us are able, we are bound by the noose of truth.
Nandishvara said: At that time Vyasa came, his head adorned with ash, wearing rudraksha ornaments, adorned with matted locks,
reciting the five-syllable mantra, filled with love for Shiva, a very mass of radiance, like a second Dharma himself.
Seeing him, they were glad, rose and stood before him, and gave him a seat beautified with kusha and deerskin.
As Vyasa sat there, they joyfully worshipped him and offered various praises, saying, "We are blessed.
The austerity well performed and the various gifts — all have become fruitful; we are satisfied by your sight, O Lord.
By your sight sorrow has gone far away, grandsire; great sorrow has been given us by wicked men of cruel deeds.
When the sight of the glorious comes, sorrow will go; it has never failed to go there — this is a considered conviction.
When one has reached the hermitage of the great, who are able in every task, if sorrow does not go, destiny alone is the cause.
There the Pandavas, relying on the vessel given by the Sun, passed their time happily indeed.
Surely poverty, the cause of sorrow, goes; this nature of the great is held to be like the wish-granting tree.
Counting only their virtues, from the great by the mere thing itself — by the power of refuge alone, O Lord, a man comes to
smallness or greatness; there is no doubt. This is the nature of the best, that they protect the lowly.
For a poor man in the world, the mark held most beneficial is striving before him and serving the good.
Beyond this is fortune; let no blame be given. For this reason, master, good has come in seeing you.
Our minds are satisfied by your mere coming; give us instruction by which our sorrow may quickly be destroyed."
Nandishvara said: Hearing these words of the Pandavas, the great sage Vyasa, glad at heart, said this:

O Pandavas, you should not grieve. You are blessed, you have done your duty, you have not abandoned truth.

Nandishvara said: Pleased by Vyasa's words, all the Pandavas, led by Yudhishthira, spoke again:
The Pandavas said: "You have spoken the truth, master: sorrow is given ceaselessly by the wicked, again and again, even in the forest, by evil-souled men.
Destroy that evil for us today and give us some good, O Lord. Krishna told us before that Shankara should always be worshipped;
we were negligent and let his words slacken; now teach us again that path of the god."
With his ten thousand disciples he joyfully asked them there for the food he desired, having come to them.
Nandishvara said: Hearing these words, Vyasa, full of joy, remembering Shiva's lotus feet, lovingly said to the Pandavas:
Vyasa said: "Hear my words today, Pandavas of righteous mind: Krishna spoke the truth; I too serve Shiva.
Serve him with love, and there will always be incomparable happiness; all sorrow indeed vanishes through the service of Shiva."
Nandishvara said: Then, considering the five for Shiva's worship, the best of sages, Vyasa, named Arjuna as fit,
and, considering the place for austerity, the best of sages then spoke again to the Pandavas, who were firm in dharma:
Vyasa said: "Listen, all Pandavas; I tell you what is ever beneficial, having seen Shiva as all and supreme, the Supreme Brahman, the goal of the good.
Whatever world is seen, from Brahma to the end of the three parardhas, all of it is Shiva's form, to be worshipped and meditated on.
He is to be served by all — Shankara, remover of all sorrow; Shiva is pleased in a short time by devotion.
Mahesha, well pleased, gives everything to devotees; he surely grants enjoyment and liberation here and hereafter.
So Shambhu should always be served by those who seek the fruit of enjoyment and liberation; Shankara is the Person himself, destroyer of the wicked, the goal of the good.
Accepting, the Pandavas sent Durvasas and the other sages and ascetics to bathe.
But first one should recite with a firm mind the vidya of Shakra; for a kshatriya of great repute this is what is enjoined.
So Arjuna should first recite the vidya of Shakra with firmness; he will test first, and then he will be pleased;
well pleased, he will always remove obstacles, and then will give the excellent mantra of Shiva himself."
Nandishvara said: Having said this and called Arjuna, he taught him the vidya of Upendra; having bathed and faced east, fierce-minded Arjuna received it.
The best of sages gave him the procedure of the earthen image, and the noble-minded Vyasa said to Dhananjaya:
Vyasa said: "Go now from here, Partha, to lovely Indrakila; staying near the Jahnavi, perform austerity properly.
May this vidya always be invisible and beneficial to you." He gave him this blessing and then said to them, the sage:
Let all of you, best of kings, stand firm in dharma; the best success will surely come; there is no doubt.
Nandishvara said: Having given this blessing to the Pandavas, the lord of sages Vyasa remembered Shiva's lotus feet and vanished in a moment.
Then all the Pandavas, for lack of food, O lord of sages, grieving, resolved in their minds to give up their lives.
Remembered by Draupadi, Krishna came at that very moment, and eating a leaf of vegetable, brought satisfaction to them [the sages].
Then Durvasas, knowing his disciples to be satisfied, went away again; the Pandavas were freed from hardship then by Krishna's grace.

Nandishvara said: While the Pandavas were grieving, the lord of sages, the ocean of compassion, the best of sages Vyasa arrived.
The Pandavas then bowed to him and worshipped him respectfully, gave him a seat and, full of sorrow, with folded hands, spoke:
The Pandavas said: "Listen, best of sages; we are burnt by sorrow, O Lord; having gained your sight today, we attain joy, O sage.
Stay here some time to destroy our sorrow, O Lord; by your sight, O brahmin sage, all sorrow dissolves."
Nandishvara said: Addressed thus, the best of sages stayed for their happiness, driving away their sorrow with various stories.
While the talk was going on with that good sage Vyasa, Dharmaraja, humble, bowing low, said this:
Dharmaraja said: "Listen, best of sages; this I hold to be the quieting of my sorrow. I ask you, greatly wise one; please tell me, O Lord:
has anyone before suffered such sorrow? We alone have met the greatest sorrow, no one else."
Vyasa said: "Long ago, to the great-souled king named Nala, lord of Nishadha, came sorrow greater than yours;
